query: An equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy has a simple solid-solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its microstructure and deformation behavior remain insufficiently understood. Under hardness testing and mechanical loading of this starting state, what single intervention could overcome the strength and hardness limitation while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics? State the proposed intervention, its mechanism, the predicted measurable change relative to the unmodified alloy, its applicable processing and test conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a microstructural and mechanical experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Addition of molybdenum to the CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy will enhance its strength and hardness through solid solution strengthening, while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with a simple solid-solution structure
generation.conditions: High-temperature tensile testing; annealing at 900 °C/50 h and 950 °C/100 h
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening due to the distortion of the lattice by Mo atoms
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased hardness and strength of the alloy
generation.boundary: The maximum amount of Mo that can be added before the alloy becomes too brittle
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Mo required to achieve the desired properties and the potential effects on ductility

falsification_experiment.design: Mechanical testing and microstructural analysis of the Mo-modified CoCrFeNiTi alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Mo does not result in increased hardness and strength, or if the alloy becomes too brittle, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Mechanism with scope. Mechanism: Molybdenum partitions to the matrix, causing solid-solution strengthening due to its larger atomic size which distorts the lattice and acts as an obstacle for dislocation movement.. System: Base alloy with 1.0 at.% Mo addition (Al 9 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 Mo 1). Conditions: High-temperature tensile testing; annealing at 900 °C/50 h and 950 °C/100 h. Evidence: inferred. Observation: The Mo-alloy exhibited round γ′-particles and lower ultimate tensile strength compared to the base alloy and Hf-alloy under the same conditions.. Scope limits: The text notes that round γ′-particles contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior, and the Mo-alloy showed the worst behavior among DS samples between 600 and 800 °C.. Alternatives: Hafnium addition which sharpens γ′-corners and reduces Heusler phase content.. Quote: "Molybdenum is supposed to partition to the matrix, to have a solid-solution strengthening effect due to its bigger atomic size and therefore to lead to a distorted lattice"
